blocks.markdown: Indigenous considerations Indigenous considerations in procurement aim to support the participation of Indigenous businesses while ensuring compliance with obligations under Comprehensive Land Claims Agreements (CLCAs) and the Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business (PSIB). While both CLCA s and PSIB promote Indigenous involvement, they are distinct frameworks with specific guidelines. Understanding how these work together is crucial, as certain procurements may be subject to both. Indigenous considerations: A unified approach Indigenous considerations in procurement are governed by both the CLCA s and the PSIB . CLCA s and PSIB are distinct and should not be confused. Key distinctions and integrations In certain cases, a procurement subject to CLCA contracting obligations may also be set-aside under PSIB . The procedures for both can be applied, provided that PSIB set-asides do not interfere with the contracting obligations under a CLCA . When conflicts arise between the two, CLCA obligations take precedence. If a CLCA grants a right of first refusal to Indigenous businesses, the procurement cannot be set-aside under PSIB . The PSIB clauses cannot be used or modified to implement the CLCA right of first refusal. If a CLCA does not include a right of first refusal, the procurement can be reserved to Indigenous businesses across Canada under PSIB while still addressing the CLCA contracting obligations, including any CLCA evaluation criteria. The act of setting aside a procurement under PSIB does not, by itself, address the CLCA procurement obligations. The various procurement obligations of the applicable CLCA will still have to be considered. A solicitation of offers subject to a PSIB set-aside that addresses CLCA evaluation criteria must clearly define what qualifies as a CLCA beneficiary. This clarification helps prevent confusion with the definition of "Indigenous business" under PSIB . Support and sourcing For help identifying potential Indigenous suppliers under PSIB set-asides, see Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business . You must make every reasonable effort to meet operational needs while achieving best value, and observing the principles of prudence, probity and sound contracting management. Duty to consult and accommodate Indigenous groups When a procurement may impact potential or established Aboriginal or treaty rights, certain responsibilities and procedures must be followed: Buyer's role You should remind clients of their duty to consult and accommodate, and you can assist by providing information on the procurement process, or by acting as an observer during the client’s consultations with Indigenous groups. However, you should not get involved in any negotiation of the procurement strategy. Client responsibilities It is the client's responsibility to comply with the legal Duty to Consult and Accommodate, when the proposed activities, to which the procurement relates, might adversely impact on potential or established Aboriginal or treaty rights. Such activities can include approvals for resource development projects, land transactions, or infrastructure developments like roads and pipelines. Accommodation measures Accommodation could involve modifications to the planned activities; terms and conditions on approvals or authorizations; financial compensation; the incorporation of Aboriginal benefits as part of the procurement strategy; etc. Consultation process This process should be completed before the client sends the requisition to PSPC as it can influence various aspects including the procurement strategy, project scope, timelines, budget, approval level required and the decision to proceed. For specific queries related to consultation, you can contact the Consultation and Information Service at Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada . Additional resources and contacts Clients seeking further guidance on consultation or accommodations should refer to Canada’s Aboriginal Consultation and Accommodation - Updated Guidelines for Federal Officials to Fulfill the Duty to Consult Further information is available through the Aboriginal and Treaty Rights Information System (ATRIS) . Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business All federal government departments are encouraged to set-aside a portion of procurements for competition by Indigenous businesses, provided operational needs are fully met. This approach aims to foster participation and competitiveness among Indigenous businesses. Despite a procurement being designated under the PSIB , all applicable procurement policies and procedures must be adhered to. PSPC buyers seeking policy guidance on PSIB can consult with the Indigenous Procurement Policy Case Management Team . You should share with IPPD any advice received from other sources to ensure a consistent approach to the implementation of PSIB . Any discrepancies in guidance must be reported to IPPD and all received advice must be thoroughly documented in the procurement file. The approval documents should include the rationale for key decisions. Set-aside program requirements for Indigenous business Indigenous businesses eligible for the set-aside program must be at least 51% Indigenous owned and controlled and can be : a band as defined by the Indian Act sole proprietorships limited companies cooperatives partnerships not-for-profit organizations Joint ventures consisting of two or more Indigenous businesses or an Indigenous business and non-Indigenous businesses are eligible if the Indigenous business has at least 51% ownership and control of the joint venture. Certification requirements The offeror must certify in its submitted offer that it is an Indigenous business or a joint venture constituted and that they meet the above ownership and control criteria as described above. As part of its offer, the offeror must complete the certification of requirements for the set-aside program for Indigenous business (certification) stating that it: meets the requirements for the program and will continue to do so throughout the duration of the contract will, upon request, provide evidence that it meets the eligibility criteria is willing to be audited regarding the certification acknowledges that if it is found not to meet the eligibility criteria, the offeror shall be subject to one or more of the civil consequences set out in the certification and the contract Additional requirements If an offer involves subcontracting, the offeror must certify in its offer that at least thirty-three percent of the value of the work will be performed by an Indigenous business. The offeror must notify the subcontractor and where applicable bind the subcontractor in writing with respect to the requirements that the Indigenous set-aside program may impose on the subcontractor. The offeror’s contract with a subcontractor must also, where applicable, include a provision in which the subcontractor agrees to provide the offeror with information, substantiating that it meets the Indigenous set-aside program requirements and also authorize the offeror to have an audit performed by Canada to verify their compliance. Failure by the offeror to exact or enforce such provision will be deemed to be a breach of contract and subject to several civil consequences, including contract termination and financial penalties. Proof of eligibility Evidence of eligibility is not required at the offer stage, but must be available for audits. The civil consequences for false statements in the offer documents, non-compliance with the requirements of the set-aside program or failing to produce satisfactory evidence to Canada regarding the requirements may include: the forfeiture of the offer deposit retention of holdbacks disqualification from future contracts potential termination of the contract with liabilities for any additional costs incurred by Canada Required evidence from businesses Documented evidence of ownership and control of an Indigenous business or joint venture may include: incorporation documents shareholders’ or members’ register partnership agreements joint venture agreements business name registration banking arrangements governance records of meeting minutes and other legal documents Ownership of an Indigenous business refers to "beneficial ownership," for example, who is the real owner of the business. Canada may consider a variety of factors to satisfy whether Indigenous persons have true and effective control of an Indigenous business. Documentation for subcontracting Evidence to support the portion of work done by subcontractors may involve contracts between the contractor and subcontractor, invoices, and payment records. The same evidence requirements apply to subcontractors as to the prime contractors to confirm they are an Indigenous business. Defining Indigenous eligibility for the purposes of set-aside program for Indigenous business Note : The word “Indian” is used within this section due to its legal context, relating to its significance in the Indian Act . For the purposes of PSIB , an Indigenous person is defined an Indian, Métis person, or an Inuk who is ordinarily resident in Canada. Evidence of being an Indigenous person includes proof such as: Indian registration in Canada membership in an affiliate of the Metis National Council or the Congress of Indigenous Peoples or other Decision to set aside When determining whether to set aside a procurement under PSIB , the decision rests with the client. There are two types of PSIB set-asides, as follows: Mandatory set-asides A procurement must be set aside under PSIB if the primary recipients or end user of the goods or services are an Indigenous population and the procurement value exceeds $5000. Provided that operational needs, prudence, probity, best value and sound contract management can be assured. For an Indigenous population to be the primary recipient or end user of the goods or services, delivery does not have to be directly to the Indigenous community. For instance, goods may be delivered to a government site before distribution to Indigenous communities, groups or individuals. Refer to Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat (TBS) Contracting Policy Notice 1996-2 for information on the meaning of Indigenous population. For examples and more information on mandatory set-asides under PSIB , please contact Indigenous Services Canada . Key distinctions and integrations In certain cases, a procurement subject to CLCA contracting obligations may also be set-aside under PSIB . The procedures for both can be applied, provided that PSIB set-asides do not interfere with the contracting obligations under a CLCA . When conflicts arise between the two, CLCA obligations take precedence. If a CLCA grants a right of first refusal to Indigenous businesses, the procurement cannot be set-aside under PSIB . The PSIB clauses cannot be used or modified to implement the CLCA right of first refusal. If a CLCA does not include a right of first refusal, the procurement can be reserved to Indigenous businesses across Canada under PSIB while still addressing the CLCA contracting obligations, including any CLCA evaluation criteria. The act of setting aside a procurement under PSIB does not, by itself, address the CLCA procurement obligations. The various procurement obligations of the applicable CLCA will still have to be considered. A solicitation of offers subject to a PSIB set-aside that addresses CLCA evaluation criteria must clearly define what qualifies as a CLCA beneficiary. This clarification helps prevent confusion with the definition of "Indigenous business" under PSIB . Support and sourcing For help identifying potential Indigenous suppliers under PSIB set-asides, see Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business . You must make every reasonable effort to meet operational needs while achieving best value, and observing the principles of prudence, probity and sound contracting management. However, you should not get involved in any negotiation of the procurement strategy. Client responsibilities It is the client's responsibility to comply with the legal Duty to Consult and Accommodate, when the proposed activities, to which the procurement relates, might adversely impact on potential or established Aboriginal or treaty rights. Such activities can include approvals for resource development projects, land transactions, or infrastructure developments like roads and pipelines. Accommodation measures Accommodation could involve modifications to the planned activities; terms and conditions on approvals or authorizations; financial compensation; the incorporation of Aboriginal benefits as part of the procurement strategy; etc. Consultation process This process should be completed before the client sends the requisition to PSPC as it can influence various aspects including the procurement strategy, project scope, timelines, budget, approval level required and the decision to proceed. For specific queries related to consultation, you can contact the Consultation and Information Service at Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada . Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business All federal government departments are encouraged to set-aside a portion of procurements for competition by Indigenous businesses, provided operational needs are fully met. This approach aims to foster participation and competitiveness among Indigenous businesses. Despite a procurement being designated under the PSIB , all applicable procurement policies and procedures must be adhered to. PSPC buyers seeking policy guidance on PSIB can consult with the Indigenous Procurement Policy Case Management Team . You should share with IPPD any advice received from other sources to ensure a consistent approach to the implementation of PSIB . Procurement strategy for Indigenous business set-aside checklist The following set-aside checklist is provided to guide you. Set-aside determination Verify if the client has indicated the procurement is set aside for Indigenous businesses. If no, and the procurement is destined primarily for Indigenous populations and exceeds $5,000, you should inform the client of the potential oversight. If no, and if qualified Indigenous suppliers exist, you should suggest the possibility of a voluntary procurement strategy for a PSIB set-aside. If no, and if neither conditions above apply, or the client confirms the procurement is not to be set-aside under PSIB , proceed as per standard procurement policies. If yes, see below. Comprehensive Land Claims Agreements (CLCA) Assess if the procurement is subject to CLCA s and determine the extent to which CLCA s and the PSIB set-aside conflict. CLCA s take precedence (see Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business ). Subcontracting to Indigenous businesses Confirm if there is a client requirement for subcontracting to Indigenous businesses. Notification Notify the Business Development Directorate, Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) , upon receipt of a set-aside requirement (see Requisition ). Solicitation of offers documentation Include the applicable documents outlined in "Requirements for the set-aside program for Indigenous business” and appropriate clauses. Sourcing Source the requirement according to established policies, procedures, and platforms (see Sourcing of requirements under the Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business (PSIB) set-asides). Notice of proposed procurement - advanced contract award notice Ensure the notice includes a statement that the procurement is set aside exclusively for Indigenous businesses (refer to the information on using a source list in Determine the sourcing strategy ). Pre-award audit Check if ISC has advised whether the procurement is subject to a pre-award audit of certifications before the solicitation closes. Certification of eligibility Verify that all offerors have provided signed certificates of eligibility with their offers (see Verify offer ). Offer evaluation Evaluate offers according to the evaluation criteria described in the solicitation of offers documents. Notification of results to ISC Inform ISC of the two "best-assessed" responsive offerors, excluding financial information. Post-audit advice Obtain advice from ISC regarding the results of the pre-award audit of certificates of eligibility. Contract award Award the contract based on established evaluation criteria and the result of the pre-award audit. Contract award notification Advise ISC of the contract award within 15 working days (see Elements to consider at award – Reporting requirements and award notices ). Contract management Manage the contract, including advising ISC of any changes in the offeror’s status as an Indigenous business or requests to verify continued eligibility. Procurement reporting Ensure accurate reporting of the set-aside under PSIB (see Elements to consider at award – Reporting requirements and award notices ).

heading_path: Buyer's Guide Socioeconomic considerations - Indigenous considerations
blocks.markdown: Under Article 800: Aboriginal Peoples of the Canadian Free Trade Agreement (CFTA), the CFTA does not apply to any measure adopted or maintained with respect to Indigenous Peoples. If a measure is adopted or maintained with respect to Indigenous Peoples and or businesses in a CFTA -covered procurement, some or all aspects of the procurement may not be subject to CFTA obligations. To reduce risk, you should continue to follow the CFTA obligations to the greatest extent possible. Deviations should be limited and only occur when necessary to implement the measure(s) for Indigenous peoples/businesses.
